changes: The card is written for Year 9 students in Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory, and needs its framing adjusted to suit Victorian Curriculum 2.0 Level 9 and the VC2E9LE01 focus on representation of places as Country.
The card's definition of Country should be tied to the Victorian context, such as Woi wurrung and Boon wurrung Country, and its example should be local to Victoria rather than generic.
match.reason: The bank card teaches the same idea of First Nations representations of Country from insider voices, but its Year 9 framing is for other states and needs Victorian localisation.

confirm.reason: The bank points on First Nations literature centre on insider voices challenging outsider portrayals or on reading works in context, and only mention Country in passing, so none teaches how these authors represent place as Country with deep links to people, culture and history.

rejected.title: Representations of place as Country
card: Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors write about a place as Country. Country is more than land. It includes water, sky, animals, plants, people and stories.
In these texts, Country is often shown as alive and as a relative or teacher. People are part of it and have duties to care for it.
Authors may show a connection that runs across generations, through family, culture and history. A place can hold memory, such as the story of an event or of an Elder.
This differs from a view of land as empty scenery or as something to own or use. Writers can show this through personification, naming, and detail that links a place to people.
rejected.remember: In many texts by these authors, a place is Country: connected to people, culture and history.

a.q: An author describes a river as an old aunt who remembers every family that has camped on its banks. What view of place does this show?
opts: Place as Country, connected to people and history
Place as empty scenery that sets the mood
Place as land that a person can own and use
Place as a danger that characters must escape
a.why: The river is shown as a relative who holds memory of people over time, which is how Country is often represented. It is not just scenery, because it has a relationship with the families.
a.clue: Look at how the river is linked to families and memory.

b.q: In a new story, Tamika returns to her grandmother's coastal home. The sea is named in her language, and the author says the shore carries her family's songs. Which choice best explains the author's effect?
opts: It presents the shore as Country with ties to culture
It presents the shore as a pleasant holiday setting
It shows that the shore is a place with little meaning
It presents the shore as land to be sold or developed
b.why: Naming the sea in language and the shore carrying songs link the place to culture and family over time. A holiday setting is the tempting answer, but nothing in the story treats the shore as only a backdrop.
b.clue: Ask what the language and songs connect the shore to.

version.title: Representations of place as Country
card: Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors represent place as Country. Country is the land, waters and skies a people belong to, with its plants, animals, stories and ancestors.
In these texts, a place is often more than a setting. Writers may show Country as living, as family, or as something people care for and are cared for by.
Country can hold history. A creek or a hill may carry stories of ancestors, of events, or of loss and survival since colonisation.

Writers can show these ties by naming places in their own languages, through personification, and with detail that links a place to family over generations. Each author writes from their own people and Country, so representations differ.
version.remember: In many of these texts, place is Country, tied to people, culture and history over time.

a.q: When an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander author represents a place as Country, what does this usually mean?
opts: The place is tied to people, culture and history
The place is a backdrop that sets a story's mood
The place is land valued mainly for what it earns
The place is wild land that no people belong to
a.why: Country is the land, waters and skies a people belong to, so a place written as Country is tied to people, culture and history. A backdrop only sets a mood, while Country is shown as more than a setting.
a.clue: Think about what Country includes besides the land itself.

b.q: In a story, a narrator walks a beach with her uncle. He names each rock in their language and tells her who in the family fished there. How does the author represent the beach?
opts: As Country, linked to family and culture over time
As a quiet setting chosen to build a calm mood
As a place the family hopes to buy and develop
As a symbol of the narrator's fear of the sea
b.why: Naming the rocks in language and linking them to family who fished there ties the beach to culture and history across generations, which is how Country is often represented. The walk may feel calm, but the details do more than set a mood: they connect the place to people.
b.clue: What do the names and the fishing stories connect the beach to?

a.best: The place is tied to people, culture and history

b.best: As Country, linked to family and culture over time
